_comment: Keyed by exact id2label strings from linkanjarad/mobilenet_v2_1.0_224-plant-disease-identification (see model/fetch_labels.py output). 'demo' classes have full curated treatment text (Stage 1 validation focus per BUILD-PLAN.md). Any other class the 38-way model predicts falls back to '_default' so the app never crashes on an out-of-scope class.

_default.description: This result is outside the app's curated disease set. Confidence and treatment guidance may be less reliable.
treatment: Isolate the affected plant if possible to limit spread.
Consult a local agricultural extension office for a confirmed diagnosis.
Retake the photo in good light, focused on a single affected leaf, for a clearer result.

Apple Scab.description: Fungal disease (Venturia inaequalis) causing dark, scabby, olive-green to brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Spreads fastest in cool, wet spring weather.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. myclobutanil, captan, or mancozeb) starting at bud break and repeating on a 7-10 day schedule through wet periods.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn — the fungus overwinters in leaf litter.
Prune to open up the canopy; better airflow speeds leaf drying and slows infection.
Plant scab-resistant varieties where replanting is an option.

Apple with Black Rot.description: Fungal disease (Botryosphaeria obtusa) causing purple-bordered leaf spots ('frog-eye leaf spot') and rotting, mummified fruit.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. captan or thiophanate-methyl) from early leaf-out through fruit development.
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and dead wood/cankers — both harbor the fungus over winter.
Prune out dead or diseased branches promptly; disinfect pruning tools between cuts.
Avoid tree stress (drought, winter injury) which makes infection more likely.

Cedar Apple Rust.description: Fungal disease (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) needing both apple and cedar/juniper trees to complete its cycle — causes bright yellow-orange spots on apple leaves.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. myclobutanil) from pink bud stage through several weeks after petal fall.
Remove nearby cedar/juniper trees if practical — spring gall growths on them are the infection source.
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties where replanting is an option.
Rake and dispose of fallen leaves to reduce overwintering spores.

Healthy Apple.description: No signs of disease detected on this apple leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially after wet spring weather.

Healthy Blueberry Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this blueberry leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.

Cherry with Powdery Mildew.description: Fungal disease (Podosphaera clandestina) causing a white, powdery coating on leaves and shoots, most visible in warm, dry weather with high humidity.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. sulfur or myclobutanil) at first sign of white powdery patches.
Prune to improve airflow and sunlight penetration through the canopy.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth mildew prefers.
Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots and leaves.

Healthy Cherry Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this cherry leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in warm, humid conditions.

Corn (Maize) with Cercospora and Gray Le.description: Fungal disease (Cercospora zeae-maydis) causing narrow, rectangular tan-to-gray lesions running parallel to the leaf veins. Worsens in warm, humid weather and in fields with heavy corn residue.
treatment: Apply a foliar fungicide (e.g. azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or propiconazole) if lesions are spreading up the plant before tasseling.
Plant resistant hybrids and rotate away from continuous corn next season.
Manage crop residue (tillage or removal) — the fungus survives in old corn debris between seasons.
Avoid excess nitrogen and overly dense planting; better airflow between plants slows spread.

Corn (Maize) with Common Rust.description: Fungal disease (Puccinia sorghi) causing reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
treatment: Apply a foliar fungicide (e.g. azoxystrobin or propiconazole) if infection is heavy before tasseling.
Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids in future seasons.
Remove volunteer corn plants that can carry the fungus between seasons.
Monitor closely — mild infections often don't need treatment.

Corn (Maize) with Northern Leaf Blight.description: Fungal disease (Exserohilum turcicum) causing long, cigar-shaped tan-to-gray lesions on the leaves. Favors moderate temperatures and extended leaf wetness.
treatment: Apply a foliar fungicide (e.g. azoxystrobin or propiconazole) if lesions are spreading before tasseling.
Plant resistant hybrids and rotate away from continuous corn next season.
Manage crop residue (tillage or removal) — the fungus survives in old corn debris between seasons.
Monitor closely — mild infections late in the season often don't need treatment.

Healthy Corn (Maize) Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this corn leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially during humid growing periods.

Grape with Black Rot.description: Fungal disease (Guignardia bidwellii) causing reddish-brown leaf spots and fruit that shrivels into hard black 'mummies'. Can destroy most of a season's crop if untreated.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. mancozeb or myclobutanil) starting early in the season, right after bud break.
Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected canes — both carry the fungus into the next season.
Prune for an open canopy to improve airflow and speed drying after rain.
Rotate fungicide chemistries across the season to avoid resistance building up.

Grape with Esca (Black Measles).description: A fungal trunk-disease complex causing 'tiger-stripe' leaf discoloration and dark spotting on berries. No fungicide reliably cures it once established in the trunk.
treatment: There is no effective chemical cure — fungicide spraying on leaves does not reach the trunk infection.
Prune out and destroy dead or symptomatic wood well below any visible staining, disinfecting tools between cuts.
In advanced cases, remove and replace the vine — it will keep declining and can spread inoculum to neighbors.
Avoid pruning during wet weather; the fungus enters through fresh pruning wounds.

Grape with Isariopsis Leaf Spot.description: Fungal disease (Pseudocercospora vitis / Isariopsis leaf spot) causing angular brown spots on leaves that can merge and cause early leaf drop.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. mancozeb) if spotting is spreading, especially in humid weather.
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves — the fungus overwinters in leaf litter.
Prune for an open canopy to improve airflow and reduce leaf-wetness duration.
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day, which extends leaf wetness overnight.

Healthy Grape Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this grape leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in humid conditions.

Orange with Citrus Greening.description: Bacterial disease (Candidatus Liberibacter spp., huanglongbing) spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, causing blotchy yellow leaf mottling and small, bitter, lopsided fruit. There is no cure.
treatment: There is no chemical cure once a tree is infected — focus shifts to preventing further spread.
Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector with a recommended insecticide program from a local extension service.
Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees promptly — they act as a source of infection for healthy trees nearby.
Source new trees only from certified disease-free nursery stock.

Peach with Bacterial Spot.description: Bacterial disease (Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni) causing small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and pitted lesions on fruit.
treatment: Apply a copper-based bactericide during dormancy and again at early leaf-out — copper is far less effective once the disease is established.
Prune for an open canopy to speed drying after rain or irrigation.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base to keep foliage dry.
Plant less-susceptible varieties where replanting is an option.

Healthy Peach Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this peach leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.

Bell Pepper with Bacterial Spot.description: Bacterial disease (Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria) causing small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and raised scabby lesions on fruit.
treatment: Apply a copper-based bactericide at first sign of spotting, repeating weekly during wet weather.
Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruit — do not compost.
Avoid working with wet plants; the bacteria spread easily on damp hands and tools.
Use disease-free seed/transplants and resistant varieties next season.

Healthy Bell Pepper Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this bell pepper leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in wet weather.

Potato with Early Blight.description: Fungal disease (Alternaria solani) causing dark concentric-ring spots on lower leaves, spreading upward.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Apply a chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicide, repeating every 7-10 days.
Rotate crops; avoid planting potatoes/tomatoes in the same soil next season.
Improve airflow between plants and avoid overhead watering.

Potato with Late Blight.description: Aggressive water-mold disease (Phytophthora infestans) — the same pathogen behind the Irish potato famine. Spreads fast in cool, wet weather.
treatment: Act immediately: remove and destroy all infected plant material, do not compost.
Apply a systemic fungicide (e.g. metalaxyl or mancozeb-based) as soon as possible.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base only.
If severe, destroy the whole plant to protect neighboring crops.

Healthy Potato Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this potato leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially after rain.

Healthy Raspberry Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this raspberry leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in humid conditions.

Healthy Soybean Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this soybean leaf.

Squash with Powdery Mildew.description: Fungal disease causing a white, powdery coating on leaves and stems, common in warm weather with high humidity.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. sulfur or myclobutanil) at first sign of white powdery patches.
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves to slow spread.
Space plants for good airflow and avoid overhead watering late in the day.
Plant mildew-resistant varieties where replanting is an option.

Strawberry with Leaf Scorch.description: Fungal disease (Diplocarpon earlianum) causing small purple spots that merge into larger scorched-looking blotches on leaves.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. captan or myclobutanil) if spotting is spreading, especially after harvest.
Remove old leaves after harvest (mowing or raking) to reduce overwintering spores.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base to keep foliage dry.
Space plants for good airflow between rows.

Healthy Strawberry Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this strawberry leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in humid conditions.

Tomato with Bacterial Spot.description: Bacterial infection (Xanthomonas spp.) causing small dark water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit.
treatment: Remove infected leaves and destroy them, do not compost.
Apply a copper-based bactericide weekly during wet weather.
Avoid working with wet plants — bacteria spread easily on damp hands and tools.
Use disease-free seed and resistant varieties next season.

Tomato with Early Blight.description: Fungal disease (Alternaria solani) causing dark target-like spots starting on older, lower leaves.
treatment: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves.
Apply a chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicide every 7-10 days.
Mulch around the base to prevent soil splash onto leaves.
Stake or cage plants to improve airflow.

Tomato with Late Blight.description: Fast-spreading water-mold disease (Phytophthora infestans) causing large greasy, dark blotches on leaves and fruit.
treatment: Act immediately: remove and destroy infected material, do not compost.
Apply a systemic fungicide (e.g. chlorothalonil or copper-based) right away.
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base only.
In severe cases, remove the whole plant to protect the rest of the crop.

Tomato with Leaf Mold.description: Fungal disease (Passalora fulva) causing pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with olive-green to gray velvety mold underneath. Common in humid greenhouses/tunnels.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. chlorothalonil or copper-based) at first sign of yellowing spots.
Improve ventilation and reduce humidity — in greenhouses/tunnels, this often matters more than spraying.
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves to slow spread.
Avoid overhead watering and wetting foliage in the evening.

Tomato with Septoria Leaf Spot.description: Fungal disease (Septoria lycopersici) causing small, circular spots with dark borders and tan centers, usually starting on lower leaves.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. chlorothalonil or copper-based) every 7-10 days once spotting starts.
Remove and destroy affected lower leaves, and clear old plant debris at season's end.
Mulch around the base to reduce soil splash onto leaves.
Stake or cage plants and avoid overhead watering to improve airflow and keep foliage dry.

Tomato with Spider Mites or Two-spotted.description: Tiny sap-sucking pests (Tetranychus urticae) causing fine yellow speckling on leaves and, in heavy infestations, visible fine webbing. Worsens in hot, dry weather.
treatment: Spray with insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or a miticide (e.g. abamectin), covering the undersides of leaves where mites live.
Rinse plants with a strong jet of water to knock down mite numbers between sprays.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft growth mites prefer.
Introduce or conserve natural predators (e.g. predatory mites, ladybugs) where possible.

Tomato with Target Spot.description: Fungal disease (Corynespora cassiicola) causing brown spots with faint concentric rings ('target' pattern) on leaves, stems, and fruit.
treatment: Apply a fungicide (e.g. chlorothalonil or azoxystrobin) once spotting is confirmed, repeating every 7-10 days.
Remove and destroy affected leaves and old plant debris at season's end.
Stake or cage plants and space them for good airflow.
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base to keep foliage dry.

Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.description: Viral disease spread by whiteflies, causing upward leaf curling, yellowing, and stunted growth. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
treatment: There is no chemical cure — remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce spread to healthy ones.
Control the whitefly vector (e.g. with insecticidal soap or a recommended insecticide) since the virus itself can't be treated directly.
Use virus-resistant tomato varieties next season where available.
Consider reflective mulch or fine mesh netting to reduce whitefly landing on young plants.

Tomato Mosaic Virus.description: Viral disease causing mottled light/dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, leaf curling, and stunted, distorted fruit. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
treatment: There is no chemical cure — remove and destroy infected plants to prevent further spread.
Wash hands and disinfect tools after handling infected plants — the virus spreads easily by contact.
Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties next season.
Control aphids and other sap-feeding insects that can spread the virus between plants.

Healthy Tomato Plant.description: No signs of disease detected on this tomato leaf.
treatment: No treatment needed.
Keep monitoring weekly, especially in humid conditions.
